pages.title: Injuries
pages.content:
WHAT WE TREAT

Injuries

Assessment at Suji starts from the region that hurts and from the training you want to return to. Six groups cover the injuries we see; fractures and surgical cases are referred on.

Six groups

Suji Sports Medicine Clinic groups the problems we assess into six: ankle and foot, knee, shin and calf, hip and groin, shoulder and elbow, and back and neck. Club athletes and amateur runners use the same list, whether the trouble showed up on an easy run, in five-a-side football, or in throwing practice. Each group is a way to start the first assessment, not a label that closes the hour.

The visit is 60 minutes. A sports physician or physiotherapist examines the region you name, then relates it to load: the treatment table first, and gait when the stride is part of the story. An Achilles tendon complaint, a sprain at the ankle, or knee pain can sit in one group and still be read against the neighbour beside it.

Taping, a follow-up, or a gait and running analysis is chosen only after that look. The fee for each of those visits is on the fees page, in US dollars.

Ankle and foot

ANKLE / FOOT

Sprains, tendon pain and a foot that will not settle in training.

Knee

KNEE

Swelling, joint-line pain and a knee that stiffens or gives after running.

Shin and calf

SHIN / CALF

Shin soreness and calf strain set against mileage, surface and push-off.

Hip and groin

HIP / GROIN

Groin and hip pain from kicking, changing direction or a long run.

Shoulder and elbow

SHOULDER / ELBOW

Overhead pain and elbow load in throwing athletes and club sport.

Back and neck

BACK / NECK

Back and neck pain that changes running, lifting or a full session.

LOWER LEG

Lower leg

Ankle, foot, shin, calf

Lower leg and foot

Ankle and foot, with shin and calf, are the lower-leg regions we see most in runners. The first picture of the clinic is this work: a clinician’s hands taping a runner’s ankle on the treatment table, and the race shoes on the floor beside the table leg.

Assessment covers how the foot sits, how far the ankle moves, and how the calf accepts a single-leg raise. A measuring tape on the calf, or a plain goniometer at the ankle, is used when a number will help the plan. A taping and strapping visit is a separate 20-minute appointment at $35 when support is needed between longer sessions.

It does not stand in for the first assessment. Later, if a graded return is the right stage, one clinic criterion is 25 single-leg calf raises on each side. That figure belongs to the return checks.

It is a criterion we record, and it is not a recovery rate.

KNEE / HIP

Knee and hip

Knee, hip, groin

Knee and hip

Knee, and hip and groin, are assessed as neighbours. Running and club sessions rarely load a single joint and leave the next one quiet.

A knee test is often done with you seated and the knee bent, so the clinician can see what the joint allows before anyone discusses mileage. Hip and groin assessment may be an assisted stretch on a low table, used to judge range and irritability rather than to finish a workout. Pain at the knee is one reason trail runners write to us; the stories page carries an anonymised composite, Yuki, 34, for that situation, and it is not a forecast for the next person through the door.

The plan, when rehabilitation goes ahead here, still has three stages: the 60-minute first assessment, rebuild across weeks 1–6 with sessions typically weekly and adjusted to the injury, and a graded return. We publish no recovery rate for knee, hip, or groin pain.

SHOULDER

Shoulder and back

Shoulder, elbow, back, neck

Shoulder and back

Shoulder and elbow, and back and neck, sit on the same fee list as the running injuries. Not every club athlete who trains here is a runner.

Leilani Kealoha, physiotherapist, works with shoulders and throwing athletes, and a shoulder assessment may include an overhead reach with the clinician’s hand on the shoulder. Lower-back assessment is often done with the patient prone and the clinician’s hands on the back, so the painful level can be found before any exercise is chosen. Neck symptoms are heard in the same visit and tied to the training week you actually do.

We do not run a separate shoulder programme with its own price. First assessment, follow-up session, gait and running analysis, taping and strapping, and the return-to-run test are the individual items. If back or neck pain follows an impact and a fracture is suspected, the next step is a referral, described in the next section, rather than another week of exercise at Millrace Road.

What we refer on

We refer on fractures and surgical cases. Those two are the list. If the assessment suggests a bone is broken, or that a surgeon should see the injury before rehabilitation continues, we say so and we do not open a rebuild plan.

Recent scans, if you already have them, belong at the first visit so existing images can be read. The clinic does not provide an imaging service, and it does not take the place of urgent care when an injury is acute and a fracture has to be ruled out the same day. A return-to-run test is not booked for a fracture, or for a case that is waiting on a surgical opinion.

When the problem is suitable for care here, booking returns to the ordinary visits: phone +00 555 0148 or hello@sujiclinic.example. Hana Lindgren, clinic coordinator, handles the diary. Early assessment slots are Tuesday and Thursday at 7:30.

Referred on, not treated here

  • Fractures
  • Surgical cases

pages.title: Method
pages.content:
HOW IT WORKS

Method

The method has three stages: Assess, Rebuild, and Return. Each stage has a set length or a set span of weeks, and the return stage ends with three clinic checks.

ASSESS

Assess

First visit, 60 minutes

Assess stage

Assess is the first visit. It lasts 60 minutes and the fee is $95.

You bring the shoes you train in, and any recent scans you already have. The hour is a clinical assessment for club athletes and amateur runners: what you were doing when the pain started, what you have tried since, and what the coming weeks of training were supposed to contain. Examination is hands-on.

An ankle may be measured, a calf palpated, a knee tested in sitting, a hip moved on the low table, a shoulder watched in an overhead reach, or a back assessed prone. Where the stride is part of the complaint, the clinician watches how you load the leg rather than stopping at the table. Dr Ingrid Solheim leads the sports physicians; Dr Tomasz Wrona is the clinic’s other sports physician.

Physiotherapists take the parts of the hour that match their roles. You leave with a plan for the next stage. A race date is not set in that hour.

REBUILD

Rebuild

Weeks 1–6

Rebuild stage

Rebuild is weeks 1–6. Sessions are typically weekly, and the spacing is adjusted to the injury rather than held to a fixed timetable for every person.

The usual item in this stage is the follow-up session: 40 minutes, $65. Strength work sits with Priya Raman, strength and conditioning coach, beside the physiotherapy team. Amara Nwosu leads physiotherapy.

Rafael Montoya works with running gait, which is why some plans add a gait and running analysis: 50 minutes, $120, with the stride watched on the treadmill. Leilani Kealoha works with shoulders and throwing athletes when the problem is not a runner’s leg. Taping, if it is useful between sessions, is the taping and strapping visit: 20 minutes, $35.

None of these items is bundled into a single package price. Each visit you book is the visit on the fee list. Weeks 1–6 describe the ordinary shape of this stage.

They are not a promise that every injury finishes at week 6.

RETURN

Return

A graded plan

Return stage

Return is a graded plan. It ends with the return-to-run test, a 45-minute visit at $80.

The clinic uses three checks, and the same three appear wherever we talk about being ready to extend easy running. Single-leg calf raises: 25 on each side. Single-leg hop distance: within 10% side to side.

Thirty minutes of easy running: pain no higher than 2 out of 10. These are clinic criteria. They record what we ask to see before the graded plan is treated as complete.

They are not a recovery rate, a prize, or a forecast of a race. Passing them means the criteria were met on the day they were tested. The return-to-run test is where those checks are brought together.

People whose assessment showed a fracture, or a case that needs surgery, are not put on this plan; they are referred on. Cancellation of any of these visits is free up to 24 hours before.

What the plan looks like

The plan is a short written line from the first hour, then the visits that follow it. It names the stage you are in, the session length you are booking, and the checks that will matter if you reach return. It does not name a medal, a club rank, or a date by which pain will be gone.

A runner who trains most days might leave Assess with weekly follow-ups across weeks 1–6, one gait analysis if the stride needs a treadmill hour, and the return-to-run test only when the graded plan is ready to be judged. A throwing athlete might have shoulder care with Leilani Kealoha in the same fee structure, without a running test until running is actually the goal. The shoes you brought stay in the story: they are the pair the plan is about.

Book each visit by phone or email. Fees are in US dollars. The clinic was founded in 2014 at 48 Millrace Road, Easthaven.

pages.title: Team
pages.content:
WHO'S IN THE ROOM

Team

Seven people work at Suji Sports Medicine Clinic. Two are sports physicians, three are physiotherapists, one is a strength and conditioning coach, and one coordinates the diary.

FOUNDER

Lead clinician

Lead sports physician, founder

Dr Ingrid Solheim

Dr Ingrid Solheim is lead sports physician and founder of Suji Sports Medicine Clinic. The clinic opened in 2014 at 48 Millrace Road, Easthaven, for club athletes and amateur runners who need assessment, rehabilitation, and return-to-run planning in one place.

Dr Ingrid Solheim

Lead sports physician, founder

She leads the clinical work of the first assessment, the 60-minute visit at $95, and the standard the room uses when a plan moves on to rebuild or return. Her portrait is the one in the corridor, in plain dark slate scrubs. The standard she holds the team to is specific: examine the injury, relate it to training, and use the published checks when a graded return is being judged. Single-leg calf raises, hop distance, and 30 minutes of easy running are clinic criteria, and she does not treat them as a promise of a result. Fractures and surgical cases are referred on, including when she is the physician in the room.

Dr Tomasz Wrona

Sports physician

Dr Tomasz Wrona is a sports physician at the clinic. He shares the assessment work with Dr Solheim: the first hour for a new injury, the decision that a problem belongs here, and the decision that it should be referred on. Fractures and surgical cases are the referrals the clinic names. In the room he examines the region in front of him, from ankle and foot through back and neck, and he ties the findings to the training the athlete is actually doing. He does not run a separate fee list. A visit with him is the same item you book with anyone else: first assessment, follow-up session, gait and running analysis, taping and strapping visit, or return-to-run test. Early slots on Tuesday and Thursday at 7:30 are open to his diary as they are to the rest of the clinical team. Hana Lindgren confirms which physician is in when you book.

Amara Nwosu

Lead physiotherapist

Amara Nwosu is lead physiotherapist. She leads the physiotherapy side of rebuild, the stage that runs weeks 1–6, typically as weekly sessions adjusted to the injury. A follow-up session with the physiotherapy team is 40 minutes and $65. Her brief is the hands-on work of rehabilitation for the six injury groups: restoring a load the athlete can repeat, and keeping the plan matched to what the assessment found. She works beside the sports physicians rather than in a separate service. When a plan needs strength coaching, she involves Priya Raman. When the stride is the question, she involves Rafael Montoya. When the athlete throws, she involves Leilani Kealoha. The return checks stay the clinic’s checks, including 25 single-leg calf raises on each side, whoever leads the session that records them. No recovery rate is published for her team.

Rafael Montoya

Physiotherapist, running gait

Rafael Montoya is a physiotherapist whose focus is running gait. He is the clinician most often beside the treadmill when a stride has to be watched, and he is the person who will usually lead a gait and running analysis. That visit is 50 minutes and costs $120. It is a separate booking from the first assessment and from an ordinary follow-up. Use it when the way the foot lands, the knee tracks, or the calf loads is part of why running is painful or uneven. He also works with the return checks that depend on a single leg: calf raises, 25 on each side, and hop distance within 10% side to side. The 30 minutes of easy running, with pain no higher than 2 out of 10, is judged with the same care. He applies those criteria to the day of the test. They are not a prediction of a race result for the runners he sees.

Leilani Kealoha

Physiotherapist, shoulders and throwing athletes

Leilani Kealoha is a physiotherapist for shoulders and throwing athletes. Club sport at Suji is not limited to running, and her sessions are where shoulder and elbow complaints are examined in depth. An assessment may include an overhead reach with her hand on the shoulder, then a plan that respects throwing load as well as any running the athlete also does. Her visits use the same items as the rest of the clinic. A first assessment is 60 minutes at $95. A follow-up is 40 minutes at $65. Taping and strapping, when a shoulder or elbow needs it between sessions, is 20 minutes at $35. She does not sell a named throwing course or a different tariff. If the findings point to a fracture, or to a case that needs surgery, she refers on, as the physicians do. Return-to-run checks are used when running is part of the graded plan, not as a substitute for a shoulder examination.

Priya Raman

Strength and conditioning coach

Priya Raman is the strength and conditioning coach. She works in the rebuild stage, once assessment has established what should be loaded and what should wait. Her sessions support the physiotherapists: single-leg strength for a runner, including the calf raises that later reach 25 on each side, and broader strength for a club athlete whose injury is at the hip, the shoulder, or the back. A visit with her is booked as a follow-up session unless you have been asked to book something else. That is 40 minutes at $65. She does not run a gym membership, and the clinic does not publish a training-package price. The spacing of her sessions follows the injury. Weekly through weeks 1–6 is typical, and it is adjusted when the assessment says a different rhythm is safer. She does not set race plans. Readiness for more running, when that is the goal, is still the return-to-run test at $80.

Hana Lindgren

Clinic coordinator

Hana Lindgren is the clinic coordinator. She runs the diary, the phone, and the inbox. Book on +00 555 0148 or at hello@sujiclinic.example. There is no form to send. She can place a first assessment, a follow-up, a gait and running analysis, a taping and strapping visit, a return-to-run test, or a club screening morning. Hours are Monday, Wednesday, and Friday 9:00–19:00, Tuesday and Thursday 7:30–19:00, and Saturday 9:00–13:00. The clinic is closed on Sunday. Early assessment slots are Tuesday and Thursday at 7:30, before work. She explains the fee before you come, in US dollars, and she notes a cancellation that is still free: up to 24 hours before the appointment. For clubs, she arranges the screening morning, up to 12 athletes, 3 hours, $480, and she records whether each athlete has consented before any note is shared with a coach.

pages.title: Stories
pages.content:
RETURNS

Stories

Three anonymised composites show how a plan is written at Suji. Each person is fictional, and each account stops at the clinic’s return checks.

How to read these accounts

Marit, Daniel, and Yuki are fictional. Each account is an anonymised composite, written so a reader can see an injury, the plan, and the checks in one place. They are not identifiable patients, and they are not testimonials.

The ages, sports, and injuries are the ones the clinic uses for these three composites and no others: Marit, 41, club marathoner, Achilles tendon; Daniel, 29, five-a-side football, ankle sprain; Yuki, 34, trail runner, knee pain. In each composite the plan follows the clinic method. Assess is the 60-minute first visit.

Rebuild is weeks 1–6, typically weekly and adjusted to the injury. Return is a graded plan ending in the return-to-run test. The checks they pass are the clinic’s checks and nothing further.

No finish time, no placing, and no recovery rate is attached to any of them.

MARIT

Achilles tendon

Anonymised composite

Marit

Marit is 41, a club marathoner, with an Achilles tendon problem. This account is an anonymised composite. In it, she books a first assessment of 60 minutes at $95 and brings the shoes she uses for club training, plus scans she already had.

Assess looks at ankle and foot together with shin and calf, because the tendon complaint loads both. Rebuild runs weeks 1–6. Sessions are typically weekly and are adjusted to the tendon.

Follow-up sessions are 40 minutes at $65. The composite includes calf work that builds toward 25 single-leg calf raises on each side, and a gait and running analysis, 50 minutes at $120, when her stride on the treadmill needs a dedicated hour. Return is graded.

She sits the return-to-run test, 45 minutes at $80, and the composite records the three checks as passed: 25 single-leg calf raises on each side, single-leg hop distance within 10% side to side, and 30 minutes of easy running with pain no higher than 2 out of 10. Those passes are criteria met inside the composite. They are not a forecast for another marathoner.

DANIEL

Ankle sprain

Anonymised composite

Daniel

Daniel is 29. He plays five-a-side football and has an ankle sprain. This account is an anonymised composite.

Assess is his first visit, 60 minutes at $95, with the shoes he wears for club play and any recent scans. The ankle is examined on the treatment table, including swelling, movement, and what the foot can accept. A taping and strapping visit, 20 minutes at $35, appears in the composite between longer sessions, as support while the sprain settles, not as the whole plan.

Rebuild is weeks 1–6, typically weekly follow-ups of 40 minutes at $65, adjusted to the sprain. Strength includes single-leg work with the physiotherapy team. Return uses the clinic’s running checks even though his sport is five-a-side, because those are the checks this clinic publishes.

In the composite he passes them on the return-to-run test at $80: 25 single-leg calf raises on each side, hop distance within 10% side to side, and 30 minutes of easy running with pain no higher than 2 out of 10. No scoreline from a match is part of the account.

YUKI

Knee pain

Anonymised composite

Yuki

Yuki is 34, a trail runner, with knee pain. This account is an anonymised composite. The first assessment, 60 minutes at $95, examines the knee in sitting, with the knee bent, and looks at hip and groin because trail running loads both.

He brings the shoes he trains in. Recent scans, if the composite’s version of him has them, are read in that hour; the clinic does not image him itself. Rebuild covers weeks 1–6, sessions typically weekly at the follow-up fee of $65 for 40 minutes, adjusted to the knee.

A gait and running analysis at $120 is included in the composite when the treadmill stride shows how the knee is being loaded. Return is graded and ends with the return-to-run test at $80 for 45 minutes. The checks passed in the account are 25 single-leg calf raises on each side, single-leg hop distance within 10% side to side, and 30 minutes of easy running with pain no higher than 2 out of 10.

The composite stops at those criteria. It does not send him back onto a named trail.

pages.title: Fees
pages.content:
PRICES

Fees

Fees are listed in US dollars for every visit the clinic books. The first hour is $95, and cancellation is free up to 24 hours before.

ASSESS

First visit

60 minutes, $95

What the first visit covers

The first visit is the first assessment. It is 60 minutes and the fee is $95, in US dollars, as are all fees on this page. That hour is the Assess stage.

It covers the history of the injury, the examination, and a plan for what happens next. Bring the shoes you train in and any recent scans. The hour can include hands-on tests for ankle, knee, calf, hip, shoulder, or back, and a first look at gait when that can be done without a separate treadmill booking.

It does not include the gait and running analysis, the return-to-run test, or a block of rebuild sessions. Those are later items with their own prices. It does not include imaging.

If the hour shows a fracture or a surgical case, we refer on, and we do not start a package of follow-ups. You book the assessment itself by phone or email. Early slots on Tuesday and Thursday at 7:30 are assessment slots, at this same fee.

Full fee list

Every fee is in US dollars. We do not convert them into another currency on this page.

The first four of these are the rows we show on the home page. The return-to-run test and the club screening morning are booked the same way, at these prices, when you need them. Follow-up sessions are the visits typically used through rebuild, weeks 1–6, and the week-to-week rhythm is adjusted to the injury. There is no discounted course that multiplies these rows into a new total. A club that wants individual care after a screening morning books those visits at the individual prices. Receipts show the item, the length, and the price you paid.

Insurance receipts

The clinic can give you a receipt for the visit you attended. The receipt names Suji Sports Medicine Clinic, the address at 48 Millrace Road, Easthaven, the item you booked, its length, and the fee in US dollars. You take that receipt to your own insurer if you wish to ask them about a claim.

We do not bill insurers, we do not name insurers, and we do not state what any policy will pay. Cover depends on the policy you hold, and the clinic does not interpret it. A receipt is available for each item on the fee list, including the club screening morning when the booking is in one name and the club asks for the paper.

Ask Hana Lindgren at the visit, or by email at hello@sujiclinic.example, if you need the receipt sent on. Phone is +00 555 0148. The receipt is a record of payment.

It is not a statement that the injury has resolved.

Cancellation

Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before the appointment. Phone +00 555 0148 or email hello@sujiclinic.example and include the name on the booking and the time of the visit. The same window applies to the first assessment, the follow-up session, gait and running analysis, taping and strapping, the return-to-run test, and a place in a club screening morning.

We do not publish a fee for a later cancellation, and we ask you to give the 24 hours whenever you can, so the slot can be offered to someone else. Tuesday and Thursday slots at 7:30 are the early assessment times; they are the ones most often wanted before work, so a free cancellation the day before is what keeps them usable. Hours for reaching the coordinator are the clinic hours: Monday, Wednesday, and Friday 9:00–19:00, Tuesday and Thursday 7:30–19:00, Saturday 9:00–13:00.

Sunday the clinic is closed, so a Monday morning visit needs the cancellation by Sunday morning if it is to stay inside 24 hours.

pages.title: Visit
pages.content:
FIND US

Visit

The clinic is at 48 Millrace Road, Easthaven. Book by phone or email, bring your shoes and any recent scans, and use the hours published below.

Address and hours

Suji Sports Medicine Clinic is at 48 Millrace Road, Easthaven. The clinic was founded in 2014. Phone +00 555 0148.

Email hello@sujiclinic.example. Hours are Monday, Wednesday, and Friday 9:00–19:00; Tuesday and Thursday 7:30–19:00; Saturday 9:00–13:00. The clinic is closed on Sunday.

Early assessment slots are Tuesday and Thursday at 7:30, before work. Those early hours are the ones named on the front of the site for the next assessment slots. The rest of Tuesday and Thursday runs on to 19:00, as Monday, Wednesday, and Friday do.

Saturday closes at 13:00, so a return-to-run test or a gait analysis on Saturday has to fit the morning. A club screening morning, 3 hours for up to 12 athletes, is placed on a day when those three hours sit inside the open diary. If you are unsure which day matches the visit you need, ask Hana Lindgren when you book.

Hours

Mon, Wed, Fri 9:00–19:00
Tue, Thu 7:30–19:00
Sat 9:00–13:00
Closed Sunday

Find us

48 Millrace Road
Easthaven

Telephone and email

+00 555 0148
hello@sujiclinic.example

FIND US

Finding us

Easthaven

Directions and parking

Come to 48 Millrace Road, Easthaven. That street number is the direction we publish.

We do not name a landmark, a bus route, or a station beside it. Plan the trip from the address itself, and allow enough time to be in the room at the start of the appointment, especially for a Tuesday or Thursday slot at 7:30. Patients who come by car park at the clinic.

We do not publish a count of spaces or a parking fee. If you are carrying scans as well as your shoes, keep them with you rather than leaving them in the car through the visit. The entrance serves the treatment rooms used for assessment and for the later stages of a plan.

Saturday visits end with the 13:00 close, so afternoon arrival is too late on that day. Sunday there is no clinic to arrive at. If the diary changes your time, Hana Lindgren confirms it by phone or email before you travel.

What to bring

Bring the shoes you actually train or race in. The work of the clinic starts from that pair: how they have worn, and what you hope to do in them again. A new pair bought only for the appointment hides the load you have been using.

Any recent scans you already have should come too, whether the problem is an Achilles tendon, an ankle sprain, knee pain, or a shoulder, back, or hip complaint. We read what you bring. We do not take new images here.

Wear something you can move in, because a calf may be palpated, a knee tested in sitting, a hip moved on a low table, or a shoulder taken through an overhead reach. If a gait hour is booked, the shoes matter even more; that visit is the 50-minute gait and running analysis. You do not need to bring a form.

Payment details and the fee for the item you booked can be confirmed before you leave home, in US dollars.

Booking by email and phone

Book by email at hello@sujiclinic.example or by phone on +00 555 0148. No form is required, on the site or at the desk. Say which visit you want, and name a day that fits the hours.

The items are the first assessment, 60 minutes, $95; the follow-up session, 40 minutes, $65; gait and running analysis, 50 minutes, $120; taping and strapping, 20 minutes, $35; the return-to-run test, 45 minutes, $80; and, for clubs, the screening morning, 3 hours, up to 12 athletes, $480. The clinic offers same-week assessments when the diary has room. Early slots are Tuesday and Thursday at 7:30.

Hana Lindgren keeps the book. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before. A receipt for insurance, if you want one, can be requested in the same email or call.

It will show the item and the US dollar fee. It will not claim that a policy will reimburse you.

pages.title: About
pages.content:
ABOUT THE CLINIC

About

Suji Sports Medicine Clinic was founded in 2014 in Easthaven for club athletes and amateur runners. The rooms are set up for assessment, rehabilitation, and a checked return to running.

Founded in 2014

Suji Sports Medicine Clinic was founded in 2014. It stands at 48 Millrace Road, Easthaven, and it has stayed a single clinic rather than a chain. Dr Ingrid Solheim is the founder and lead sports physician.

The people who work with her now are Dr Tomasz Wrona, sports physician; Amara Nwosu, lead physiotherapist; Rafael Montoya, physiotherapist for running gait; Leilani Kealoha, physiotherapist for shoulders and throwing athletes; Priya Raman, strength and conditioning coach; and Hana Lindgren, clinic coordinator. The founding purpose has not been replaced by a second service. This is a sports medicine clinic for club athletes and amateur runners.

Fees are still the six published items, in US dollars, from the $95 first assessment to the $480 club screening morning. The phone and email have remained the way in: +00 555 0148 and hello@sujiclinic.example. The year 2014 is the founding year we state.

We do not attach a patient count or an award to it.

WHY

Why this clinic

Founded in 2014

Why this clinic exists

The clinic exists so that assessment, rehabilitation, and return-to-run planning can happen in one room of people who share the same criteria. Club athletes and amateur runners were arriving with pain that rest had quieted and with shoes they still wanted to use.

Rest fixes the pain. It rarely fixes the reason. Suji was founded in 2014 in Easthaven to look for that reason and to set a way back that can be checked.

The line we use is simple: the shoes are waiting, and we set the way back. The way back is Assess, then Rebuild across weeks 1–6, then a graded Return. The checks at the end are 25 single-leg calf raises on each side, a single-leg hop within 10% side to side, and 30 minutes of easy running with pain no higher than 2 out of 10.

We publish those numbers because they are the bar we use. We do not publish a recovery rate beside them. Fractures and surgical cases are referred on, because this clinic was not founded to replace a surgeon or an emergency department.

The rooms

How the treatment rooms are arranged

The rooms are arranged so that a single visit can move from the table to a running task when the plan calls for it. Hands-on assessment and taping happen on a treatment table: an ankle being taped, a calf palpated, a knee tested, a back assessed, a shoulder reached overhead. A treadmill is in the clinic for the gait and running analysis and for watching a stride during ordinary care.

A step is there for single-leg calf raises, and a floor mark is there for the hop. The 30 minutes of easy running that belongs to the return checks is planned with the clinician; the clinic does not describe itself as the owner of an outdoor track. Dr Solheim’s portrait hangs against the pale corridor that links these rooms.

Nothing in the arrangement is a spa, and nothing is a gym floor with a membership. You are here for the visit you booked, at the length and the US dollar fee on the list, and then you leave. The coordinator’s desk is where the diary, the receipt, and the consent for a club report are handled.

pages.title: Athletes & Clubs
pages.content:
ATHLETES & CLUBS

Athletes & Clubs

Clubs book a screening morning for up to 12 athletes, or they send athletes to ordinary visits. A coach sees a report only when that athlete has consented.

CLUBS

Club arrangements

For club athletes

Club arrangements

Suji Sports Medicine Clinic works with club athletes as well as with people who train on their own. A club arrangement is a booking made in advance, usually through a coach or a club volunteer, for a screening morning or for a run of individual visits.

Individual visits stay on the ordinary fee list: first assessment $95 for 60 minutes, follow-up $65 for 40 minutes, gait and running analysis $120 for 50 minutes, taping and strapping $35 for 20 minutes, and the return-to-run test $80 for 45 minutes. All of those prices are in US dollars. The clinic does not offer a cheaper club tariff for those items, and it does not sign agreements with named federations.

Dr Ingrid Solheim leads the clinical side. Hana Lindgren coordinates dates. The club contact writes to hello@sujiclinic.example or calls +00 555 0148.

Athletes from the club still book their own follow-up if they want care after the morning, unless the club is paying and has said so in the booking.

Screening morning

The club screening morning takes up to 12 athletes and lasts 3 hours. The fee is $480, in US dollars, for the morning as a whole. It is the sixth item on the fee list, and it is not a substitute for a first assessment when one athlete has a new injury that needs a full hour.

Clinicians see athletes in turn during the three hours. The work is a screen for club training, not a same-morning rebuild plan and not the return-to-run test. If someone needs that test, or a gait and running analysis, it is booked as its own visit at its own price.

Weeks 1–6 of rehabilitation are not packed into the morning. Coaches who want the early part of the day should know the clinic’s early slots for ordinary assessments are Tuesday and Thursday at 7:30; the screening morning itself is arranged on a date the diary can hold for three hours. Cancellation of the morning is free up to 24 hours before, on the same rule as every other booking.

Reports and consent

A coach receives a report about an athlete only with that athlete’s consent. Consent is recorded before the note is shared, and it belongs to the athlete, including when the club has paid the $480 for the morning. Without consent, the clinic can confirm attendance to the person who booked, and it does not pass on findings, checks, or recommendations.

With consent, the report covers what was seen at the screening and whether an individual visit is advised. It does not include a recovery rate, a ranking inside the club, or a clearance to play that claims more than the visit can support. The return checks, when they have actually been done in a separate return-to-run test, can be included for that athlete: 25 single-leg calf raises on each side, hop distance within 10% side to side, and 30 minutes of easy running with pain no higher than 2 out of 10.

Those figures stay criteria, not a verdict on selection. Hana Lindgren is the person who checks that consent is present before anything is sent.

pages.title: FAQ
pages.content:
QUESTIONS

FAQ

Answers below use the clinic’s hours, fees, and return checks. If your question is about your own injury, book a first assessment rather than relying on a general note.

Who is the clinic for?

Suji Sports Medicine Clinic is for club athletes and amateur runners. That includes people in a club, people who train without one, and athletes whose sport is not only running, such as five-a-side football or throwing, when the injury still fits the work we do. We assess six groups: ankle and foot, knee, shin and calf, hip and groin, shoulder and elbow, and back and neck. Dr Ingrid Solheim founded the clinic in 2014 at 48 Millrace Road, Easthaven, and remains lead sports physician. A club can also book a screening morning for up to 12 athletes. If you are looking for a fracture service or for care that should sit with a surgeon, we are the wrong place, and we will say so. The method, when we do see you, is Assess, Rebuild, and Return. You do not need a referral form to request a first assessment. You do need an injury or a training problem you want examined.

What happens in a first assessment?

The first assessment is 60 minutes and costs $95, in US dollars. It is the Assess stage. Bring the shoes you train in and any recent scans. A sports physician or physiotherapist takes the history and examines the region: hands on an ankle, a knee in sitting, a calf, a hip, a shoulder, or a back. Gait is considered when the complaint appears in running. You leave with a direction for the next stage. Rebuild, if that is the direction, is weeks 1–6, typically weekly, adjusted to the injury. Return, later, is a graded plan ending in the return-to-run test. The first hour does not include that test, and it does not include the separate gait and running analysis unless you have booked that item instead. If the findings point to a fracture or a surgical case, the plan stops and we refer on. The fee is for the assessment hour, not for a course of care bundled in advance.

What do visits cost?

All fees are in US dollars. We do not convert them. First assessment: 60 min, $95. Follow-up session: 40 min, $65. Gait and running analysis: 50 min, $120. Taping and strapping visit: 20 min, $35. Return-to-run test: 45 min, $80. Club screening morning, up to 12 athletes: 3 hours, $480. Home shows the first four rows; the full list is these six. Follow-ups are the sessions typically used in weeks 1–6, and we do not multiply them into a prepaid package with a new price. A screening morning does not include six individual assessments inside the $480. After the morning, an athlete who wants a full first hour books it at $95. Receipts show the item, the length, and the fee. Ask hello@sujiclinic.example or call +00 555 0148 if you want the price repeated before you book. The price on the list is the price charged for that item.

When are you open?

Monday, Wednesday, and Friday we are open 9:00–19:00. Tuesday and Thursday we are open 7:30–19:00. Saturday we are open 9:00–13:00. We are closed on Sunday. The early slots are Tuesday and Thursday at 7:30, and they are the assessment times we point to for people who want to come before work. Saturday’s close at 13:00 means an afternoon visit cannot be placed that day. A club screening morning needs a 3-hour block inside these hours. The phone, +00 555 0148, and the email, hello@sujiclinic.example, are answered in these hours by Hana Lindgren, the clinic coordinator. A cancellation still has to meet the 24-hour rule even when the clinic is shut the day before your visit, so count back from the appointment time rather than from the next morning we are open. The address is 48 Millrace Road, Easthaven, if you are checking that you have the right clinic before you set out.

How do I book, and what should I bring?

Book by phone on +00 555 0148 or by email at hello@sujiclinic.example. There is no form. Name the visit, and say if you want an early slot on Tuesday or Thursday at 7:30. Same-week assessments are offered when the diary has room. Bring the shoes you actually use, not a pair bought for the day, and bring recent scans if you have them. Wear clothes that allow an examination of the area that hurts. You do not need to bring a referral, a club letter, or a payment in a set form beyond what Hana Lindgren confirms when you book. Fees are in US dollars at the published rates, from $35 for taping and strapping up to $480 for a club screening morning. If a coach will receive any note afterwards, the athlete’s consent has to be given; say so when you book and the coordinator will record it. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before.

What if I need to cancel?

Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before the appointment. Contact the clinic on +00 555 0148 or at hello@sujiclinic.example, and give the name and the time of the visit. The rule is the same for a first assessment, a follow-up, a gait and running analysis, taping and strapping, a return-to-run test, and a club screening morning. We do not publish a separate late-cancellation charge. We do ask for the 24 hours, because Tuesday and Thursday at 7:30 are the early slots other people are waiting to use, and a screening morning holds up to 12 athletes for 3 hours. Sunday the clinic is closed, so if your visit is early Monday, send the cancellation by the matching hour on Sunday if you want it to fall inside the free window. Hana Lindgren updates the diary. If you are moving the visit rather than dropping it, say which of the open hours you can do instead, and she will look for a same-week assessment when one is free.

Do you treat fractures or injuries that need surgery?

We refer on fractures and surgical cases. That is the whole of the referral list we publish. If a first assessment, or any later visit, suggests a bone is broken, or that a surgeon should give an opinion before rehabilitation continues, we stop the rebuild plan and say so. We do not tape a suspected fracture and review it next week as a substitute for that referral. We do not provide imaging, so bring recent scans if they already exist, and seek urgent care when an acute injury needs a fracture ruled out the same day. The return-to-run test is not used as a clearance for these cases. The rest of our work, for injuries that do belong here, continues as usual: ankle and foot, knee, shin and calf, hip and groin, shoulder and elbow, back and neck. Being referred on is a clinical decision in the room. It is not a comment on the seriousness of your sport, and it does not come with a recovery rate for the injury we are sending elsewhere.

What are the return-to-run checks?

Three checks are the clinic criteria at the end of a graded return. Single-leg calf raises: 25 on each side. Single-leg hop distance: within 10% side to side. Thirty minutes of easy running: pain no higher than 2 out of 10. They are recorded at the return-to-run test, which is 45 minutes and costs $80. They are criteria for that stage of the plan. They are not a recovery rate, and they are not a promise about the next race or the next match. The anonymised composites of Marit, Daniel, and Yuki are written so that each of them meets these three checks and no extra ones. Rebuild usually comes first: weeks 1–6, sessions typically weekly and adjusted to the injury, often as 40-minute follow-ups at $65. A gait and running analysis, $120 for 50 minutes, may sit earlier if the stride needs the treadmill. Meeting the checks means the numbers were reached on the test. It does not mean every later run will be painless.

NOTES FROM THE ROOM

Journal

The journal is a place for notes on assessment and rebuild. The first note, on the three return checks, is published below.

Notes from the clinic

The journal is where the clinic writes down how it assesses and rebuilds, in ordinary language, for club athletes and amateur runners. The notes are from Suji Sports Medicine Clinic at 48 Millrace Road, Easthaven, founded in 2014. They do not announce awards, name real patients, or quote a recovery rate.

The three people on the stories page, Marit, Daniel, and Yuki, stay there as anonymised composites; the journal does not add further cases. Fees, when a note mentions them, are the published ones, in US dollars. Clinical criteria, when a note mentions them, are the three return checks: 25 single-leg calf raises on each side, single-leg hop distance within 10% side to side, and 30 minutes of easy running with pain no higher than 2 out of 10.

A note can explain what a check is for. It cannot promise that meeting the check will produce a particular season. Questions about your own injury belong in a booked visit, not in a comment on a page.

posts.title: 25 calf raises, a hop, and 30 easy minutes
posts.excerpt: The return stage at Suji ends with three clinic checks, and those checks are criteria for a plan, not a forecast of a race.
posts.content:
The shoes are waiting. Most people who write to Suji Sports Medicine Clinic already know which pair they mean. They are club athletes and amateur runners, and they want a way back to the training those shoes were for. The clinic was founded in 2014. It is at 48 Millrace Road, Easthaven. The work is assessment, rehabilitation, and return-to-run planning. This note is about the last of those, and about the three checks we use before easy running is extended.

Rest fixes the pain. It rarely fixes the reason. A quieter week can settle symptoms, and many people need that week before they call. When they do book, the first assessment still asks what the tissues were doing: the surface, the session, the shoes, and whether the same complaint has shown up in the calf, the ankle, or the knee. That visit is 60 minutes. The fee is $95, in US dollars, like every other fee in this note. Bring the shoes you actually train in. Bring recent scans if you have them. The clinic does not take new images.

Dr Ingrid Solheim, lead sports physician and founder, sets the clinical standard for that hour, with Dr Tomasz Wrona, sports physician, and the physiotherapy team. Amara Nwosu leads physiotherapy. Rafael Montoya works with running gait. Leilani Kealoha works with shoulders and throwing athletes when the person in the room is not only a runner. You leave Assess with a direction. A race date is not chosen in that hour.

Rebuild is the middle stage. It covers weeks 1–6. Sessions are typically weekly, and the spacing is adjusted to the injury. The usual booking is a follow-up session, 40 minutes at $65. Strength work sits with Priya Raman, strength and conditioning coach, alongside the physiotherapists. Single-leg calf raises are often part of that strength, long before anyone is asked for 25. Some plans add a gait and running analysis, a separate visit of 50 minutes at $120, when the stride has to be watched on the treadmill. Taping, when it is useful between sessions, is its own visit: 20 minutes, $35. Each of these is a separate item. The clinic does not sell them as a discounted block.

Return is a graded plan, and it ends with the return-to-run test. That test is 45 minutes and costs $80. Before it is treated as passed, three checks have to be met. They are the same three wherever the clinic writes about readiness.

Single-leg calf raises: 25 on each side. The raise is done one leg at a time, so a stronger calf cannot hide a weaker one. Twenty-five is the count we ask for on the day. It is a clinic criterion. It does not mean the Achilles tendon, or any other tissue, is settled after that day.

Single-leg hop distance: within 10% side to side. The two sides are compared with each other. The check is the gap between them, not a distance copied from someone else’s training. Within 10% means the weaker side is close to the stronger side on that test.

Thirty minutes of easy running: pain no higher than 2 out of 10. The running is easy, and the pain score has a ceiling. A run that stays under that ceiling for 30 minutes meets the check. A run that climbs above 2 out of 10 does not, even if the runner finishes the half hour. The score is what the person reports on the day. We do not translate it into a permission to enter a race.

Taken together, the three checks say that a single leg can raise, a single leg can hop with the two sides close, and easy running can be kept inside a low pain score for half an hour. That is all they say. They are not a recovery rate. They are not an award. They are not a statement about next season. Passing them means the criteria were met when they were tested.

The stories of Marit, Daniel, and Yuki are anonymised composites, and they are fictional. Marit is 41, a club marathoner, with an Achilles tendon problem. Daniel is 29, he plays five-a-side football, and he has an ankle sprain. Yuki is 34, a trail runner, with knee pain. Each account is written through Assess, Rebuild, and Return, and each composite passes these three checks and no others. They are there so the plan can be read. They are not quotes from identifiable patients.

We refer on fractures and surgical cases. If that is what an assessment shows, the graded plan is not started, and the return-to-run test is not used as a workaround. The six injury groups we do take on — ankle and foot, knee, shin and calf, hip and groin, shoulder and elbow, back and neck — still have to clear that line.

If you want the test, book it on its own, after the graded plan has reached that point. If you have not been seen here before, the first booking is the assessment, not the test. Hana Lindgren, clinic coordinator, keeps the diary. Phone +00 555 0148 or email hello@sujiclinic.example. There is no form. Hours are Monday, Wednesday, and Friday 9:00–19:00, Tuesday and Thursday 7:30–19:00, and Saturday 9:00–13:00. Sunday the clinic is closed. Early assessment slots are Tuesday and Thursday at 7:30. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before.

Bring the shoes. The raises, the hop, and the easy half hour are how we decide whether the way back has reached this clinic’s bar. They are a clear bar. They are not a promise past it.
